fields.lessonRecap: The governor-general was a leading colonial official acting under the Spanish Crown, not an elected president of an independent republic. The office had civil and military responsibilities; people, resources and actions determined how duties were performed. Issuing an order, delivering it and implementing it are separate events. Implementation means putting it into practice. The Real Audiencia de Manila was a court with additional governmental roles; its existence does not prove universal fairness. An official record can establish an order without establishing delivery, equal benefit or every household’s experience.

expected.content:
The governor-general was a leading official of the Spanish colonial government, acting under the authority of the Spanish Crown. The Crown means the monarchy and its authority, not only the object worn on a head. This office belonged to colonial government, not to a modern elected Philippine presidency.

An office and a person are different. Different people could hold the office at different times. Knowing one name does not explain all its responsibilities or establish that every holder acted identically. The arrangements of government also changed over the long colonial period.

Try a fictional museum-caption task. A caption calls the governor-general the elected president of an independent Philippine republic. Correct the relationship: this was an official of an outside colonial monarchy. Do not replace one misleading title with a claim that the official could act without laws or other institutions.

Our diagram is a simplified relationship guide, not a complete chart for every year.

The elected president of a modern independent Philippine republic
A leader chosen identically by every local community
A person without any relationship to the monarchy

fields.content:
The governor-general held a leading office in Spanish colonial government. The Spanish Crown means the monarchy and its authority, not just a royal headpiece.

An office and its holder are different: several people can hold the same position at different times. Responsibilities and government arrangements also changed over the long colonial period.

Try a fictional museum label: replace “elected president of an independent republic” with the correct colonial relationship. This does not mean the official could ignore laws or other institutions. The diagram is a simplified guide, not a chart for every year.

expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: The office had civil and military responsibilities carried out through many participants
expected.content:
Central government involved administration, resources and defense. The governor-general held broad responsibilities, including the military role associated with captain-general. Broad responsibilities did not mean one person personally carried out every task. Officials, navigators, messengers and local participants all mattered.

A responsibility tells what an office was meant to do. It does not prove how well a duty was performed. To investigate performance, ask what decisions were made, who acted and what consequences followed.

Watch how to sort a fictional record. A description of an office's defense duty names a responsibility. A later report about supplies reaching a particular place concerns an action and its result. Keep those categories separate before evaluating the official.

The examples are classroom exercises, not recovered orders. Later missions examine local offices and particular systems; this scene introduces central responsibilities without claiming that one chart describes every year or that all communities experienced government identically.

expected.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Use them to explain your choice.
expected.content:
A central decision did not travel by itself. Written messages, officials and resources connected a governing center with particular places. An order's issue, delivery and implementation are separate events. Implementation means putting a decision into practice.

Your earlier investigations showed why a colonial base did not establish immediate control everywhere. The same question applies here: where and when was a decision carried out, and how did people respond? A central-government chart describes relationships; it is not evidence that every arrow worked perfectly.

Try a fictional worked example. A record shows an order was issued in Manila. A second record shows that a messenger delivered it elsewhere. Neither alone tells whether it was put into practice there. Seek evidence of the later action and local responses.

Do not invent a universal response or treat distance as the only factor. Resources, relationships, knowledge and resistance could shape what happened. Local government and Indigenous leadership are the next mission's focus.

fields.title: Issued, delivered or carried out?
fields.content:
A decision did not travel by itself. Written messages, officials and resources connected Manila with other places. Implementation means putting a decision into practice.

Try fictional records: one says an order was issued in Manila, another says a messenger delivered it. Neither alone proves the order was carried out. Look for the later actions and local responses.

Distance was not the only influence. Resources, relationships, knowledge and resistance could shape the outcome. A chart’s arrow does not prove all those connections worked perfectly.

expected.content:
The Real Audiencia de Manila was an institution with judicial and other governmental functions. Judicial means connected with courts and judging legal matters. The Supreme Court's historical account describes it as a court with additional executive, advisory and administrative roles.

The governor-general also served as its presiding officer in the historical arrangement described by that account. Do not imagine two entirely unrelated boxes that never shared responsibilities. At the same time, a court and a governor's office are different concepts, and neither is the whole of government.

For this fictional exhibit task, compare a caption saying the governor was the only institution with a source naming the Audiencia. Correct the caption while keeping a limit: the existence of an institution does not prove that all decisions were fair or that every person had equal access to justice.

This is an introductory overview. Institutional powers and arrangements changed; our simple guide is not a modern separation-of-powers chart or an unchanged structure for every colonial year.

fields.content:
Judicial means connected with courts and judging legal matters. The Real Audiencia de Manila had judicial and other governmental functions, including advisory and administrative roles in the historical account used here.

The governor-general also presided over it in the arrangement described. A court and a governor’s office are different concepts even where responsibilities overlap. Their relationship is not a modern separation-of-powers diagram.

expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Separate the recorded order from the unproven claim about effects
expected.content:
A record can tell us what an official ordered without telling us every effect. It may emphasize a duty, an intended result or the official's own explanation. Local accounts and evidence of actions can help test the claim.

The Library of Congress discussion of colonial relationships highlights local interests and connections. This helps us ask who participated and whose viewpoint is missing from a simple account of central power. It does not mean all official records are useless; it means their claims need careful reading.

Work through a fictional report: the governor ordered supplies moved, so every household benefited equally. The first clause describes an order. The second needs separate evidence about delivery, implementation and effects on people. A good report states the gap rather than fills it with an invented speech.

Ask what the record establishes and what remains uncertain. The office's broad power did not make every resident's experience identical, and criticism of a particular action does not make all people in a group the same.

fields.title: An order is not everyone’s experience
fields.content:
A record may emphasize an official’s duty or intended result. Evidence about actions and local responses helps investigate what followed. An official account can be useful without containing every viewpoint.

Try a fictional report: “Supplies were ordered, so every household benefited equally.” The order is one claim. Delivery and effects on particular households need more evidence. State that gap instead of inventing a speech or one response for everyone.

expected.content:
Explain central government without turning it into one person doing everything. Identify the governor-general's relationship to the Spanish Crown. Connect a responsibility with the people and resources needed to carry it out. Distinguish an issued decision, its delivery and its implementation.

Include the Audiencia as another institution with judicial and other roles. Do not force the arrangement into a modern government chart or assume the existence of a court proves fairness for all. Keep period, place and the limits of the source in your explanation.

Use this fictional report frame in your own words: The office represented [authority]. Its responsibilities included [duty]. The evidence records [action], but we need [further evidence] to assess its effects on [affected people]. This is a classroom guide, not an original speech.

fields.content:
The governor-general was a leading colonial official acting under the Spanish Crown, not an elected president of an independent republic.

The office had civil and military responsibilities; people, resources and actions determined how duties were performed.

Issuing an order, delivering it and implementing it are separate events. Implementation means putting it into practice.

The Real Audiencia de Manila was a court with additional governmental roles; its existence does not prove universal fairness.

An official record can establish an order without establishing delivery, equal benefit or every household’s experience.

Try this fictional report frame: The aim was [aim]. At [place and time], people used [action]. Evidence shows [result], while [claim] still needs evidence.

expected.content:
A decision from a central office needed people working in particular places. Provincial and town responsibilities connected colonial institutions with communities. A diagram can help identify these levels, but it cannot prove that every order was carried out.

The NCCA overview describes provincial posts such as alcalde mayor and corregidor. These were offices within colonial administration, not labels for every person living in a province. Use a fictional message exercise. A central office issues instructions, a provincial official receives them, and a town record reports an action. Identify the level of each record before asking what happened to people. Do not treat a modern provincial governor or mayor as an exact substitute for a historical office.

The next questions concern responsibilities and evidence, not memorizing a complete list of officials.

expected.content:
The gobernadorcillo was a town-level official during Spanish colonial rule. The title is different from governor-general, the central office studied in Mission 1. Similar-looking words can refer to different responsibilities.

The San Andres municipal government's historical overview describes the gobernadorcillo as a leader of a pueblo, or town, with administrative and other duties. That local overview is a starting source, not proof of identical practice in every town for the whole colonial period. Selection rules and titles changed over time.

Try a fictional museum-label task. A caption says the gobernadorcillo governed the whole colony from the central government. Correct the level before making a larger claim. Next ask which records show the actions of that official in the town.

Do not infer every resident's approval from an officeholder's title or describe historical selection procedures as the same as modern universal elections. The lesson introduces the role; it does not reconstruct one election for every period.

fields.content:
A pueblo is a town. The gobernadorcillo was a town-level official with administrative and other duties. Its similar-sounding name does not make it the governor-general’s central office.

The municipal source offers one local overview. Check a town’s period and records rather than assuming identical selection or duties everywhere. Historical procedures were not the same as modern universal elections.

expected.content:
Local leadership did not begin with Spanish offices. Earlier missions introduced organized communities and their leaders. Colonial rule could draw on local leaders and prominent families while changing relationships of power. Continuity means something carried on; change means something became different. Both can appear in one history.

The Library of Congress discussion describes the importance of prominent local people, or principales, alongside other participants in colonial relationships. Principal?a refers to a privileged local group in the colonial setting. It was not a name for every Indigenous person or proof that all communities followed the same political path.

Cabeza de barangay is another local office title encountered in colonial records. Do not assume its duties were identical to a present-day barangay position or to every earlier datu's role. Ask which setting and rules a record describes.

Use a fictional comparison: a family maintains local influence but holds a new colonial office. Identify continuity of influence and change of institutional relationship without saying that nothing changed or that all earlier leadership vanished.

fields.content:
Local leadership existed before Spanish offices. Colonial institutions could draw on prominent local people and families while changing relationships of power.

Principalia refers here to a privileged local group, not every Indigenous person. Cabeza de barangay is another colonial office title; its duties should not be assumed identical to a modern barangay position or every earlier datu’s role.

Try a fictional family case: local influence continues, but a member holds a new colonial office. Identify continuity of influence and change in institutional relationship. Avoid saying either nothing changed or all earlier leadership vanished.

expected.content:
An intermediary helps connect people or institutions. Local officials could communicate demands and information between colonial authorities and communities. That position could involve responsibilities, privileges and pressure. It does not establish that an intermediary agreed with every demand or represented every resident equally.

In the National Archives town-record collection, requests involve town officials and principales. Such records show local participants using administrative processes. A request is evidence of an action, not automatically evidence that the request succeeded or that everyone supported it.

Work through a fictional case: a town record reports a demand for supplies, and another document requests a change. Identify the demand and the response separately. Do not invent the result if no later record is supplied. This is a classroom exercise, not a quotation from the archive.

Later missions examine tribute and other systems in detail. Here, follow the relationship: who communicated, who was affected, what action is recorded and what remains unknown?

expected.content:
A list of officials tells us who held listed positions. It does not by itself tell us how fairly they acted or what every household experienced. A petition may preserve the voice of its writers while leaving other people's views absent.

The National Archives describes records containing requests, decrees and local administrative material. Their variety helps historians investigate actions and relationships. Each document still needs its own date, setting and purpose. Do not assume that a later record reconstructs every earlier community.

Try a fictional source check. An official reports that an instruction was carried out, but a household record describes difficulty meeting it. The accounts need not answer the same question. Ask what action each records and compare the evidence instead of discarding a voice because it differs from an official account.

A report should identify whose information survives and what further evidence is needed. Do not treat all local officeholders as either heroes or villains solely because of their title; evaluate particular actions and consequences.

fields.lessonRecap: Encomienda involved rights to collect tribute from specified people or communities, with stated obligations. Land claims need separate evidence. expected.title: A Right to Collect, Not Automatic Land Ownership
expected.content:
Encomienda was a colonial arrangement involving rights to collect tribute from specified people or communities, with stated obligations attached. An encomendero was a holder of such a grant. The name of the arrangement should not be read as an automatic deed transferring every piece of community land.

Distinguish the questions: who could demand tribute, who lived in the area, and who held rights in land? They are connected but not identical. Records about collection do not alone settle every land claim. This introduction does not say that land dispossession never occurred; it says that the particular claim needs appropriate evidence.

Try a fictional exhibit label. It calls an encomienda a private estate that automatically made every field and every person the holder's property. Correct the definition and identify what further records would be needed about land or treatment of people.

The diagram describes relationships, not an exact territorial map or a title deed.

fields.content:
An encomendero held an encomienda grant. The arrangement concerned tribute collection from specified people or communities, with obligations attached. Do not turn the name into an automatic deed to every field or ownership of people.

Ask separately: who could collect, who lived there, and what rights existed in land? Saying these are different questions does not mean dispossession never happened. A particular land claim still needs the appropriate evidence.

expected.content:
Tribute was a payment required under colonial authority. It could be demanded in money or goods according to the rules and circumstances involved. Do not call a demanded payment a voluntary gift simply because an account uses a favorable label.

Forms, rates and arrangements changed across periods and settings. This lesson does not give one universal amount, modern currency conversion or identical rule for every household. Ask the date, place and terms of the record before making a numerical claim.

Use a fictional comparison. One person freely offers a present. Another household is told a payment is required by an authority. Identify what makes these different. The exercise is not a transaction that students must perform and does not award points for extracting resources from people.

A payment record can help investigate collection, but its existence does not reveal every family's ability to pay or show that every person approved of the requirement.

expected.title: Stated Duties and Actual Practice
expected.content:
Colonial justifications connected tribute collection with obligations such as protection and religious instruction. A stated duty is evidence of what was expected or claimed, not proof that it was fulfilled. Students can study a religious obligation historically without being asked to practise the religion.

Late-sixteenth-century discussions of tribute debated collection and obligations. These records help show that practice could be disputed even within colonial institutions. The debate is not a complete record of every local voice and does not establish identical conditions in all communities.

Watch how to check a fictional report. A grant lists a duty, while another record describes an unfulfilled promise. Keep the formal expectation and evidence of performance separate. Do not assume the grant proves fair treatment or that a complaint proves the same event happened everywhere.

Ask who wrote the claim, what action is recorded and what further evidence could show the experience of the people affected.

expected.discoveryText: Investigate demands, actual collection and household circumstances separately. A fictional illustration cannot establish universal historical burdens.
expected.imageCaption: Modern teaching diagram, not an original historical source.
expected.content:
Collection affects people, not only the totals recorded by officials. To examine an effect, ask what was demanded, what was collected and what resources remained for the people involved. A record of revenue and a record of household circumstances answer different questions.

Try a fictional classroom example. A household has a supply of goods, and a required collection removes part of it. The example supports a change in those goods. It does not supply an authentic historical rate or show the circumstances of every family. No arithmetic amount in this exercise should be treated as a real tax schedule.

The burden would need evidence about resources and circumstances, not only an amount. People could seek relief, negotiate, adapt or resist. Identify a particular action rather than assume a single response from everyone.

Explain the evidence without turning an official's total into every household's feelings or using a fictional family to stand for all communities.

fields.title: Follow what remained for a household
fields.content:
Ask what was demanded, what was collected and what remained for the people involved. Official revenue and household circumstances answer different questions.

Anderson’s study examines a 1597 Ilocos investigation involving tax collector Francisco Salgado. It records complaints about extra collections and pressure on communities. This is a named case, not proof of the same experience everywhere.

Now try a fictional household: some stored goods are taken as required payment, leaving fewer. That models a resource effect, not a real tax schedule. Resources, family circumstances and responses are needed before judging the burden.

expected.content:
A grant, collection account and complaint are different kinds of evidence. The grant may describe rights and duties. The account may record receipts. The complaint may describe a disputed practice or request a change. Do not make one document answer every question.

An official account and a critic's argument both have purposes and viewpoints. Historical discussions of tribute preserve disagreements, but affected people's experiences may still be incompletely recorded. Compare claims and evidence rather than assuming an official title guarantees fairness or every complaint was resolved.

Try a fictional source check. A complaint says a collection was excessive, while the available record contains no reply. You can report that the complaint was made. You cannot invent the final decision or treat the absence of a reply as proof of every person's consent.

Keep place and time attached to the claim. This lesson introduces evidence questions; it does not settle every land dispute, collection rate or history of resistance.

fields.content:
Encomienda involved rights to collect tribute from specified people or communities, with stated obligations. Land claims need separate evidence.

Tribute was a required payment under colonial authority. Its forms and rules need a particular place and period.

Collection was linked in colonial justifications to duties such as protection and religious instruction; actual performance needs evidence.

Collection could affect household resources. A particular example cannot establish every family’s burden or response.

expected.content:
Reduccion was a colonial policy of gathering or relocating people into more concentrated settlements. The word could also refer to the settlement itself. A pueblo is a town. This lesson investigates reorganization, not a claim that communities first appeared when a town was established.

People already had homes, work, relationships and knowledge of their surroundings. An official plan to gather them changed the relationship between settlement and colonial institutions. A planned move does not show that everyone moved, agreed or had the same experience.

Try a fictional record check. One card orders a group to move nearer a center. Another shows a proposed settlement. These support a plan, not every family's actual location afterward. Seek separate evidence of implementation and effects.

The diagram is a teaching model, not a reconstruction of a particular town. Do not read its houses as a count of real residents or its lines as exact historical routes.

expected.content:
Colonial officials and missionaries sought settlements that made administration, religious instruction and collection easier to organize. These are aims to investigate, not proof that everyone benefited or that every aim was fulfilled. A religious purpose can be studied historically without requiring students to practise a faith.

NCCA's discussion of Cordillera history connects settlement concentration with conversion and tribute collection in that setting. It is one regional discussion, not a single unchanged rule for all communities. Avoid turning the officials' purposes into everyone's wishes.

Watch how to classify a fictional planning statement: officials want households closer to institutions so contact can be organized. The statement supports an administrative aim. A later claim that every household found life easier needs evidence about those households.

Explain why an authority sought a change while keeping its actual effects and the people's responses separate. Naming an aim does not justify coercion or show that a move was freely chosen.

Officials and missionaries sought concentrated settlements to help organize administration, religious instruction and collection. The NCCA Cordillera discussion connects concentration with conversion and tribute in that regional setting.

Try a fictional statement: officials want households nearer institutions. Classify an administrative aim. Whether families found life easier needs different evidence. A religious aim can be studied without practising the faith, and naming a purpose does not justify coercion.

expected.decisionExplanation: Plans and rules describe intended arrangements. Actual buildings, residence and use require separate evidence.
expected.content:
A plan can show how a settlement was intended to be arranged. A central open space and nearby institutions can help explain the organizing idea of a town center. But a simplified teaching layout is not a survey of every actual pueblo.

The NCCA source book presents translated colonial legislation about settlements. A rule or design instruction tells us what an authority prescribed. It is different from a later record of what was built, where people stayed or how spaces were used. Dates matter: a law compiled in one period does not automatically describe every earlier settlement.

In this fictional map-reading exercise, identify the center, houses and paths. Ask what each symbol represents, then state what is absent: scale, actual travel times and complete household evidence. Do not convert an easy-looking line into proof that every family could reach work conveniently.

To investigate a named place, compare plans with records of buildings, residence and daily activity. The design alone cannot answer every question.

fields.content:
A town plan may show a central open space, institutions, houses and paths. The teaching layout explains an organizing idea; it is not a survey of every pueblo.

A translated colonial design instruction tells what was prescribed. Check its date rather than apply it automatically to every earlier town. To investigate implementation, look for what was built, occupied and used.

Try a fictional plan-reading task: identify symbols and connections, then note missing scale and travel information. A line on the plan cannot establish exact walking time or every household’s access to work.

expected.keyTermDefinition: The recurring activities through which people work and live.
expected.imageAlt: A conceptual teaching guide for A Move Can Affect Daily Work. It does not establish a real town layout, household count, travel time or every community's experience.
expected.imageCaption: Modern teaching diagram, not an original historical source.
expected.content:
Where people live can affect access to fields, water, fishing, paths and relatives. To investigate a settlement move, ask about daily routines as well as the location of institutions. A change that helps one task may complicate another.

Try a fictional household example. A new residence is nearer an office but farther from the family's usual work site. This illustrates two possible relationships; it is not a recovered family history or evidence that all households faced identical distances. Without a scale or travel record, do not invent minutes or kilometers.

Compare the authority's aim with the household's circumstances. Ask who moved, what resources were available and how work was maintained. Effects need evidence about particular people, place and time. The policy label alone cannot establish whether a family experienced an advantage, a burden or both.

A report should keep missing information visible rather than assign one experience to all people. This activity examines consequences; students do not earn points for displacing households.

expected.title: People Responded to Reorganization
expected.content:
A settlement policy was not a machine that moved everyone in the same way. People could negotiate, adapt, resist or maintain connections outside a proposed center. What they actually did needs evidence about their setting. Do not assume all communities accepted a plan, or that every response was identical.

Town records and requests preserved by the National Archives can help investigate local changes and participation. A petition asking for a change is evidence of a request, not proof of the decision or that every resident shared it. A colonial official's report may emphasize compliance while other evidence raises questions about actual residence.

Use a fictional source comparison: one record gives an order and another asks to revise it. Identify the plan and the response before judging the outcome. If no reply or later residence evidence is supplied, do not invent it.

The aim is to explain human choices and the policy's limits, without describing people who maintained other settlement patterns as less worthy or without organization.

Use this fictional report frame in your own words: Authorities planned [change] for [stated aim]. Evidence from [place and period] shows [action or response]. To assess daily effects and actual residence, we still need [further evidence]. This is a classroom tool, not an original quotation.
